precepts.text: Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not, and fire from the LORD devoured them; only the appointed could burn the incense on this altar.
precepts.point: Then Moses said unto Aaron, This is it that the Lord spake, saying, I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me, and before all the people I will be glorified. And Aaron held his peace.

note.label: Exodus 37: Bezaleel Makes the Ark, the Mercy Seat, and the Holy Furniture

precepts.why:
On the incense altar the Lord required that special incense, “the pure incense of sweet spices, according to the work of the apothecary”, one who compounded such mixtures: a special sweet mixture of spices to be used only for the tabernacle, burned consistently on this altar. None other was to be burned on it, and it was a matter of life and death.

“And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the Lord, which he commanded them not. And there went out fire from the Lord, and devoured them, and they died before the Lord.”

They were not the ones authorized to burn the incense. In the tabernacle service you had to be appointed to do certain services; you could not just take it upon yourself to do them. Then Moses said unto Aaron, this is it that the Lord spake, saying, I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me, and before all the people I will be glorified; and Aaron held his peace.

precepts.text: Aaron shall burn a perpetual sweet incense throughout your generations, and no strange incense; the law of the incense was already set.
precepts.point: The fire that went out from the Lord was the same fire that came out from before the Lord in Leviticus 9 and consumed the burnt offering upon the altar.

note.label: Leviticus 10: Strange Fire and the Charge of the Priesthood

precepts.why:
The instructions for the incense were already given before Nadab and Abihu ever took up their censers. “And Aaron shall burn thereon sweet incense every morning: when he dresseth the lamps, he shall burn incense upon it. And when Aaron lighteth the lamps at even, he shall burn incense upon it, a perpetual incense before the Lord throughout your generations.”

And the restriction: “Ye shall offer no strange incense thereon, nor burnt sacrifice, nor meat offering; neither shall ye pour drink offering thereon.” There were instructions on what could be burned and what could not. The strange fire is that Nadab and Abihu put strange incense before the Lord, “which he commanded them not.”

When the Most High gave instructions through Moses on what to sacrifice and how, it was with specificity; you were to do it exactly the way he told you. The law of the incense was already set, and they went outside it.

precepts.text: Zacharias, a righteous priest of the course of Abia, had the burning of incense as his lot; each Levite was appointed his own service.
precepts.point: The fire that went out from the Lord was the same fire that came out from before the Lord in Leviticus 9 and consumed the burnt offering upon the altar.

note.label: Leviticus 10: Strange Fire and the Charge of the Priesthood

precepts.why:
Nadab and Abihu were also not the ones authorized to burn the incense. In the tabernacle service you had to be appointed to certain services and could not take a service upon yourself. Zacharias shows the pattern throughout the generations: “a certain priest named Zacharias, of the course of Abia”, righteous before God, “walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless.”

“And it came to pass, that while he executed the priest’s office before God in the order of his course, According to the custom of the priest’s office, his lot was to burn incense when he went into the temple of the Lord.” He executed the office in the order of his course, and his lot, his appointed job, was to burn incense. Each Levite was appointed his own service. Nadab and Abihu took up the censer that was not their lot, and offered what was not commanded.

precepts.text: There came a fire out from before the Lord that consumed the offering on the altar; that is the fire that devoured Nadab and Abihu.
precepts.point: The fire that went out from the Lord was the same fire that came out from before the Lord in Leviticus 9 and consumed the burnt offering upon the altar.

note.label: Leviticus 10: Strange Fire and the Charge of the Priesthood

precepts.why:
“And there went out fire from the Lord, and devoured them.” That is the same fire from the chapter before: “And there came a fire out from before the Lord, and consumed upon the altar the burnt offering and the fat: which when all the people saw, they shouted, and fell on their faces.”

The fire that came out from before the Lord and consumed the burnt offering upon the altar in Leviticus 9 is the fire that devoured Nadab and Abihu in Leviticus 10. The same fire accepted the offering that was done as commanded, and consumed the priests who offered strange fire “which he commanded them not.”

precepts.text: Make no mourning for the dead; the Most High took Ezekiel's wife and he was not to weep for her.
precepts.point: The same standard fell on Jehoiakim the son of Josiah: they shall not lament for him, saying, Ah my brother, or, Ah lord.

note.label: Leviticus 10: Strange Fire and the Charge of the Priesthood

precepts.why:
Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar were told, “Uncover not your heads, neither rend your clothes; lest ye die, and lest wrath come upon all the people.” Basically they were told not to mourn for Nadab and Abihu, because they died in the midst of sin and what they did was abominable to the Most High.

Ezekiel is the example of that word. “Son of man, behold, I take away from thee the desire of thine eyes with a stroke: yet neither shalt thou mourn nor weep, neither shall thy tears run down. Forbear to cry, make no mourning for the dead, bind the tire of thine head upon thee, and put on thy shoes upon thy feet, and cover not thy lips, and eat not the bread of men.”

The Most High took away the desire of his eyes, his wife, with a stroke, and he was not to weep for her. “So I spake unto the people in the morning: and at even my wife died; and I did in the morning as I was commanded.” Ezekiel went and taught the people that morning, and at even his wife died, and he made no mourning, just as the priests were commanded.

precepts.text: Concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: they shall not lament for him.
precepts.point: The same standard fell on Jehoiakim the son of Josiah: they shall not lament for him, saying, Ah my brother, or, Ah lord.

note.label: Leviticus 10: Strange Fire and the Charge of the Priesthood

precepts.why:
The same standard fell on a king. “Therefore thus saith the Lord concerning Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah; They shall not lament for him, saying, Ah my brother! or, Ah sister! they shall not lament for him, saying, Ah lord! or, Ah his glory!”

Concerning Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, they shall not lament for him. As Aaron and his sons were not to uncover their heads or rend their clothes for Nadab and Abihu, who died in the midst of sin, so no one was to lament for Jehoiakim. Whom the Most High judges in sin is not to be mourned over.

precepts.text: Neither shall he go out of the sanctuary, for the crown of the anointing oil of his God is upon him; that is why they could not leave.
precepts.point: They were not to go out from the door of the tabernacle, for the anointing oil of the Lord was upon them. The anointing oil had already been put on them, so they could not leave the sanctuary.

note.label: Leviticus 10: Strange Fire and the Charge of the Priesthood

precepts.why:
Aaron and his sons were told, “ye shall not go out from the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, lest ye die: for the anointing oil of the Lord is upon you.” The law of the priests says the same: “Neither shall he go out of the sanctuary, nor profane the sanctuary of his God; for the crown of the anointing oil of his God is upon him: I am the Lord.”

The anointing oil had already been put on Aaron and his sons, so they could not leave the sanctuary, not even for the death of Nadab and Abihu. The crown of the anointing oil of his God is upon him; that is why they could not leave, “And they did according to the word of Moses.”

precepts.text: The sons of Zadok that kept the charge of the sanctuary shall come near to minister unto the Most High and keep his charge.
precepts.point: On the priests' hair: they were not to shave their heads nor suffer their locks to grow long, but only poll their heads. Polling the head means keeping the hair trimmed and maintained; you can grow it, but keep it up.

note.label: Leviticus 10: Strange Fire and the Charge of the Priesthood

precepts.why:
Some read Leviticus 10:9 and think Aaron and his sons could never drink at all. Going precept upon precept, Ezekiel lays out the priests’ work rules and shows what it really speaks of.

“the priests the Levites, the sons of Zadok, that kept the charge of my sanctuary when the children of Israel went astray from me, they shall come near to me to minister unto me.” They “shall enter into my sanctuary, and they shall come near to my table, to minister unto me, and they shall keep my charge.” That is the priest at work, doing the Lord’s work, the same work Aaron and his sons were charged with in the tabernacle of the congregation.

So the rule about wine belongs to the time they went in to minister. It is the charge of the sanctuary, the priest on the job, that the rest of Ezekiel 44 goes on to lay out.

precepts.text: In the inner court they wear linen and nothing that causeth sweat, and going out to the people they put off the garments wherein they minister; the priest's uniform for the Lord's work.
precepts.point: On the priests' hair: they were not to shave their heads nor suffer their locks to grow long, but only poll their heads. Polling the head means keeping the hair trimmed and maintained; you can grow it, but keep it up.

note.label: Leviticus 10: Strange Fire and the Charge of the Priesthood

precepts.why:
When the priests entered the gates of the inner court they were clocking in. “they shall be clothed with linen garments; and no wool shall come upon them, whiles they minister in the gates of the inner court, and within.” They had “linen bonnets upon their heads” and “linen breeches upon their loins”, and “they shall not gird themselves with any thing that causeth sweat.” That is the priest’s uniform for the Lord’s work.

“And when they go forth into the utter court, even into the utter court to the people, they shall put off their garments wherein they ministered, and lay them in the holy chambers, and they shall put on other garments.” Going out to the people, they took the uniform off, like taking off a work uniform at the end of a shift.

That is the frame for Leviticus 10:9. The Lord spoke of when they went “into the tabernacle of the congregation”: on duty, in the uniform, doing the work. That is when there was no drinking.

precepts.text: Neither shave the head nor suffer locks to grow long, but poll the head; keep the hair trimmed and maintained.
precepts.point: On the priests' hair: they were not to shave their heads nor suffer their locks to grow long, but only poll their heads. Polling the head means keeping the hair trimmed and maintained; you can grow it, but keep it up.

note.label: Leviticus 10: Strange Fire and the Charge of the Priesthood

precepts.why:
Among the priests’ work rules the Lord also sets their hair: “Neither shall they shave their heads, nor suffer their locks to grow long; they shall only poll their heads.”

Polling the head means keeping the hair trimmed and maintained. They were not to shave it bald, and they were not to let it grow long and wild. You can grow it, but keep it up.

It sits right alongside the linen garments and the rule about wine, all part of the charge the priest kept when he came in to minister.

precepts.text: Neither shall any priest drink wine when they enter into the inner court; no drinking on the job.
precepts.point: On the priests' hair: they were not to shave their heads nor suffer their locks to grow long, but only poll their heads. Polling the head means keeping the hair trimmed and maintained; you can grow it, but keep it up.

note.label: Leviticus 10: Strange Fire and the Charge of the Priesthood

precepts.why:
“Neither shall any priest drink wine, when they enter into the inner court.” That is exactly what Leviticus 10:9 speaks of: “Do not drink wine nor strong drink, thou, nor thy sons with thee, when ye go into the tabernacle of the congregation, lest ye die.”

Ezekiel puts the same rule in the same place, at the entering in of the inner court, where the priest is clothed in his linen and at work. It does not say the priests could never drink; it says there was no drinking on the job. When they went in to do the Lord’s work, they went in sober.

precepts.text: They teach the difference between the holy and profane and stand in judgment in controversy; the priest must be sober dealing with the people.
precepts.point: On the priests' hair: they were not to shave their heads nor suffer their locks to grow long, but only poll their heads. Polling the head means keeping the hair trimmed and maintained; you can grow it, but keep it up.

note.label: Leviticus 10: Strange Fire and the Charge of the Priesthood

precepts.why:
Here is why the priest had to be sober minded. “they shall teach my people the difference between the holy and profane, and cause them to discern between the unclean and the clean.” That is the very charge of Leviticus 10:10-11: “that ye may put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean”, and “that ye may teach the children of Israel all the statutes which the Lord hath spoken unto them by the hand of Moses.”

“And in controversy they shall stand in judgment; and they shall judge it according to my judgments.” When there was a dispute among the people, the priest stood as judge, and he judged by the judgments of the Most High, not his own. He kept the laws and statutes in all the assemblies and hallowed the sabbaths.

A man who is teaching the people and judging their controversies cannot be drinking. Dealing with the people, the priest must be sober; that is the reason behind the wine rule.

precepts.text: The fat with the breast is brought and the breast waved for a wave offering before the Lord; that is the wave offering of this passage.
precepts.point: The wave offering is explained in chapter 7: his own hands shall bring the offerings of the Lord made by fire, the fat with the breast, that the breast may be waved for a wave offering before the Lord.

note.label: Leviticus 10: Strange Fire and the Charge of the Priesthood

precepts.why:
Moses told Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar that the wave breast and heave shoulder were theirs to eat in a clean place, “thou, and thy sons, and thy daughters with thee”, their due by a statute for ever. Chapter 7 explains what the wave offering is.

“His own hands shall bring the offerings of the Lord made by fire, the fat with the breast, it shall he bring, that the breast may be waved for a wave offering before the Lord.” The man bringing his peace offering carries the fat with the breast, and the breast is waved before the Lord.

That is the wave breast of Leviticus 10:14-15, brought “with the offerings made by fire of the fat, to wave it for a wave offering before the Lord”, and given to Aaron and his sons as their portion.

precepts.text: The law of the sin offering: the priest that offereth it for sin shall eat it in the holy place.
precepts.point: Those were the instructions of the law of the sin offering: the priest that offereth it for sin shall eat it in the holy place, and all the males among the priests shall eat thereof; but no sin offering whereof any of the blood is brought into the tabernacle to reconcile withal shall be eaten, it shall be burnt in the fire.

note.label: Leviticus 10: Strange Fire and the Charge of the Priesthood

precepts.why:
Moses was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar because the goat of the sin offering was burnt when it should have been eaten. These were the instructions he was holding them to: “This is the law of the sin offering: In the place where the burnt offering is killed shall the sin offering be killed before the Lord: it is most holy.”

“The priest that offereth it for sin shall eat it: in the holy place shall it be eaten, in the court of the tabernacle of the congregation.” The Most High had given the sin offering to the priests “to bear the iniquity of the congregation, to make atonement for them before the Lord”, and eating it in the holy place was part of that work.

So when Moses asks, “Wherefore have ye not eaten the sin offering in the holy place, seeing it is most holy”, he is pointing them straight back to this law, “as I commanded.”

precepts.text: All the males among the priests shall eat thereof, but a sin offering whose blood is brought into the tabernacle is burnt, not eaten.
precepts.point: Those were the instructions of the law of the sin offering: the priest that offereth it for sin shall eat it in the holy place, and all the males among the priests shall eat thereof; but no sin offering whereof any of the blood is brought into the tabernacle to reconcile withal shall be eaten, it shall be burnt in the fire.

note.label: Leviticus 10: Strange Fire and the Charge of the Priesthood

precepts.why:
“All the males among the priests shall eat thereof: it is most holy.” The sin offering was food for the priests, eaten in the holy place, and that is what Eleazar and Ithamar should have done with the goat.

There is one exception: “no sin offering, whereof any of the blood is brought into the tabernacle of the congregation to reconcile withal in the holy place, shall be eaten: it shall be burnt in the fire.” When the blood goes into the tabernacle, the offering is burnt, not eaten.

That is exactly the point Moses makes: “Behold, the blood of it was not brought in within the holy place: ye should indeed have eaten it in the holy place, as I commanded.” The blood of this goat did not go in, so the exception did not apply, and the goat was to be eaten, not burnt.

precepts.text: Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire which the Lord commanded them not, and fire from the Lord devoured them; I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me.
precepts.point: Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, offered strange fire before the Lord which He commanded them not, and fire went out from the Lord and devoured them; that is what reverencing the sanctuary means.

note.label: Leviticus 26: The Blessings and the Curses

precepts.why:
This is what reverencing the sanctuary means. Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, “offered strange fire before the Lord, which he commanded them not. And there went out fire from the Lord, and devoured them, and they died before the Lord.”

When you came into the sanctuary you had better come with respect, because the Most High was putting men to death over it. Moses gave the reason: “This is it that the Lord spake, saying, I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me, and before all the people I will be glorified.” And Aaron, their father, held his peace.

So keeping the sabbaths of the Most High and reverencing His sanctuary go together, and the fire that came out on Aaron’s own sons shows how seriously He takes the second one.

precepts.text: Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire before the Lord, which he commanded them not, and fire from the Lord devoured them.
precepts.point: Nadab and Abihu died when they offered strange fire before the Lord; go back and read that account.

note.label: Numbers 26: The Second Census of the Families of Israel

precepts.why:
“And Nadab and Abihu died, when they offered strange fire before the Lord.” Go back and read that account.

“And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the Lord, which he commanded them not. And there went out fire from the Lord, and devoured them, and they died before the Lord.”

They offered strange fire which He commanded them not, and fire from the Lord devoured them. That is why the census names only Eleazar and Ithamar of Aaron's sons still standing.
